newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan official downplays trade gap issue at G7.
newsitem.headline: Japan official downplays trade gap issue at G7.

text.p: Japan's external trade surplus is unlikely to be a major political issue at a meeting of the leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations later this month, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazuo Ogura said on Tuesday.
"I don't think that the G7 leaders will specifically discuss Japan's trade surplus and it is not likely to be a major political issue at the summit," he said in an interview.
The G7 summit is due to be held from June 20 to 22 in Denver, Colorado, with Russia participating in its political discussions.

Ogura, who has been involved in preparations for the summit, said finance ministers of the G7 members -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- may bring up the trade issue.
U.S. officials have expressed concern about a renewed surge in Japan's trade surplus, which rose a hefty 163 percent in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.

Ogura said the United States is most interested in seeing if Japan's economic recovery will continue, and if so, Washington would like to see growth that is led by domestic demand and not driven by exports.

Japan's economy is not in a situation now where it can hurt other G7 economies, Ogura said. "What is more important for the world economy is whether the U.S. economy will make a soft landing without inflation and whether Europe can smoothly achieve monetary union," he said.
The group may issue two separate statements at the end of the meetings -- one on economic issues by the G7 and another on political issues by the G7 plus Russia, he said.
Ogura said every G7 nation is interested in stability in exchange rates, but added he doubted if G7 leaders would hold a specific discussion on currency issues.
On international financial matters, the G7 will discuss how to strengthen cooperation among central banks and finance ministries in their supervision of financial institutions, Ogura said.
Cooperation with rapidly developing countries is needed in an international effort to prevent the kind of financial problems that rocked Mexico in 1994/95, he said.
